match.reason: Neither bank point teaches regular English plural patterns (-es, y to ies, f to ves, irregular plurals); one covers deliberate spelling for effect and the other borrowed-word spelling from other languages, so neither teaches the same idea.

note:

Some style guides allow apostrophes in plurals of single letters (mind your p's and q's), so 'does not make a plural here' or 'is not used for plurals of nouns like bench' would be safer.

rejected.title: Spelling plurals
card: Most nouns add -s, but nouns ending in s, x, sh or ch usually add -es: fox becomes foxes, church becomes churches. When ch sounds like k, just add -s: stomach becomes stomachs.
If a noun ends in a consonant and then y, change the y to ies: city becomes cities. If a vowel comes before the y, just add -s: day becomes days.
Many nouns ending in f or fe change to ves: leaf becomes leaves, wolf becomes wolves, knife becomes knives. Some, such as roof, just add -s: roofs.
Some plurals change completely: child becomes children, mouse becomes mice, foot becomes feet. A few do not change at all, such as sheep.
rejected.remember: Check the ending of the noun, then pick the pattern. Learn the odd ones.

a.q: What is the plural of the noun "berry"?
opts: berries
berrys
berryes
berrees
a.why: Berry ends in a consonant and then y, so the y changes to ies. Adding only -s is tempting, but that pattern is for a vowel before the y, as in days.
a.clue: Look at the letter before the y.

b.q: Which sentence spells every plural correctly?
opts: The wolves left their paw prints near the benches
The wolfs left their paw prints near the benchs
The wolves left their paw prints near the bench's
The wolfs left their paw prints near the benches
b.why: Wolf changes to wolves, and bench ends in a ch that does not sound like k, so it takes -es to make benches. The other sentences miss one of these changes or add an apostrophe, which never makes a plural.
b.clue: Check the ending of each noun in turn.
